articles.title: Resource competition intensifies with surge in megaconstellations
articles.author: Hope Hodge Seck

paras.en: Amazon wants more than 5,000 satellites in orbit. Blue Origin has proposed another 5,400. Chinese companies have filed plans encompassing vastly more. Elon Musk has talked about a constellation numbering 1 million.
There is one issue: building all of them.

The unprecedented rush to put satellites into low Earth orbit is colliding with shortages of specialized components and materials, suppliers struggling to keep up and competition from the booming artificial intelligence industry. The squeeze is forcing satellite companies to rethink designs, accept delays and confront a more fundamental question about the timelines for what’s possible.

Competition for scarce resources and supplies amid surging demand is forcing tradeoffs in industry that threaten to delay launches and may push companies out of the market or trigger greater consolidation.

“Companies right now are just looking at where they might be able to take additional risk,” said Steve Jordan Tomaszewski, vice president of space systems for the Aerospace Industries Association. He participated in a supply chain analysis with audit firm PricewaterhouseCoopers earlier this year that involved talking to dozens of industry representatives.

Tomaszewski said supply chain challenges have companies looking for “where they can maybe downgrade something to not using a space-qualified component … Maybe they’re okay waiting a year for a certain type of valve because they know that’s going to be something they really have to deliver on.”

The 54-page analysis isolated nine critical components contributing to supply chain bottlenecks due to an inability to keep up with demand, ranging from valves and actuators to switchgears and transformers. The report incorporated insights from about 30 professionals representing various parts of the satellite supply chain.
“We hear from companies that because demand is so high and capacity is not keeping up with demand,” Tomaszewski said. “That’s what’s forcing them to really make some of those hard decisions.”

According to some estimates, the next few years could mean the nearly 19,000 satellites now in LEO joined by 70,000 more. And while analysts who spoke with SpaceNews were, across the board, unwilling to speak to companies’ plans and challenges on the record, they agreed that the coming demand signal will only exacerbate already-felt bottlenecks around limited and necessary resources.

As space companies face a ramp-up in competition from Earth-based data centers for the minerals and materials they need to launch megaconstellations, experts say something’s got to give, in the form of delays, industry consolidation, material substitutions or favorable new policies. And, amid increasing global instability, certain industry shocks could be sudden and severe.
One bottleneck stems from access to the rare earth minerals that are crucial for electronic components.

Carla Filotico, partner and managing director at the European consulting firm Novaspace, told SpaceNews she’s particularly concerned about gallium nitride (GaN) and germanium, two minerals used to build high-efficiency solar cells. For common satellite materials like aluminum, the possibility of running out isn’t much of a concern, she said.

“If we assume an average of 500 kilos of mass per satellite, and we make a pure calculation of the amount of aluminum necessary, we can say that, from the primary aluminum production that is currently quite large globally, this space sector is still a niche,” Filotico said.

Space applications make up a few percent of the market demand for GaN, on the other hand, and China’s chokehold on production, at around 98%, leaves U.S. and European companies vulnerable, she said. China is also a dominant producer of germanium, for which space applications make up an even larger market share.
She added that any restrictions on gallium export could cause a shortage for the space sector that could hit at any time.
Even aluminum has become more scarce and costly amid shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the U.S.-Iran conflict.

“Supply chain resilience has been a topic that has been very popular since COVID, but it’s just accelerated with more and more of these conflicts and disruptions,” said Doug Anderson, a partner at PwC’s Operations and Supply Chain Services practice who collaborated on the joint AIA report on space supply chain bottlenecks, released in March.
“The Strait of Hormuz has impacted aluminum, has impacted helium. These are things that are very important for the space supply chain,” he said.

It’s a problem with a dangling threat but no clear solution, although the last year has seen efforts to establish new mineral supply pipelines, such as a May 2025 agreement between defense prime RTX and Emirates Global Aluminum to start up gallium production in Abu Dhabi. Filotico said the worst of the resource squeeze is likely to be felt in the next five years, with the planned peak of the new constellation launch wave set to hit by 2030.
A trade disruption or geopolitical crisis that disrupts access to GaN and germanium “could certainly cause space sector shortage,” Filotico said.

And megaconstellations, due to the realities of scaling and maintenance, exacerbate the hazard of a sudden disruption to mineral supply. At one to two solar arrays per satellite, a single megaconstellation can easily require 10,000-20,000 solar panels.
“We are talking about thousands of satellites per company per year at least, because you need to replenish the satellites every four or five years, depending on the orbital height,” Filotico said.
The PwC-AIA analysis earlier this year revealed, among other things, that parts shortages are due not only to an inability to move faster and produce more, but also an unwillingness to do so.

The report described suppliers who were passing up changes to bid on space work, “citing high complexity requirements and low return on effort.” It described one case specifically in which a legacy supplier opted not to rebid on making composite overwrapped pressure vessels, needed to store high pressure gases, because the work would take about one-third of all the available engineering time while only generating “low single-digit revenue.”

At the Air Force Association’s Air Space & Cyber conference in September, Gurpartap “GP” Sandhoo, director of the Space Development Agency, said his organization continues to face supply-chain throughput and quality problems as it builds out its missile-tracking and data-transport constellations.
“We have had a demand signal, but the quality control and being able to produce things at scale has been a challenge,” Sandhoo said.

He pointed to optical communications hardware and focal-plane arrays as areas where suppliers have struggled with throughput, as well as the difficulty of manufacturing hardware that can withstand launch.

Compounding the challenges, Tomaszewski said, are a surfeit of parts pipelines with just one or two suppliers, leading to single points of failure, and new customer competition in the form of AI data centers.

Some suppliers are approaching changing buying patterns by designing parts that can scale to perform in both critical and risk-tolerant mission scenarios, Ken Stoler, a space business development lead for Arrow said on SpaceNews’ Space Minds podcast. He argued that a strong supply chain must be resilient and diverse.

The demand for data centers has notably increased even in the months since the supply chain report was released, he said, and the builders of those centers may represent a more attractive and profitable customer for suppliers of critical components than satellite constellation-makers. With switchgears and transformers specifically, the report found AI companies were “gobbling these things up at scale” and creating years-long parts backlogs.

“For a space company to come in and say, ‘Hey, we want to buy 10 of these for a new factory’ — compare that to … a big artificial intelligence company or data center company buying 10,000 of these things,” Tomaszewski said.
“The scale of it, even with the surge in space, isn’t big enough to kind of change the trajectory of where those electrical boxes are going.”

A challenge to broader efforts to ensure space companies have what they need to execute on their launch plans is a consistent and continual way to measure available resources, he said. There’s no guarantee, he added, that the nine critical components highlighted in March would still be at the top of the list today, and no simple way to find out.

“It’s been the problem with space that there hasn’t been kind of consistent awareness of where those issues are across programs, across you know national security space, civil space and commercial space,” Tomaszewski said.

That kind of data could also make it easier to enact policy interventions. For example, Tomaszewski proposes a “skip the line” authority that would allow the space industrial base to get in front of data centers and other competitors for resources.

“If we want to deliver on all these great capabilities from space and explore the solar system and beat China, you know, back to the moon, we might need to make sure that space is prioritized amongst all the other national priorities that we have,” he said.

Tomaszewski said he was encouraged by steps from the federal Office of Space Commerce to allow government and industry players to strategize over supply chain issues and discuss possible regulatory moves that could help.

“One big thing I think really still needs to get figured out is where the belly button is for fixing supply chain issues, especially at different government agencies,” he said. “Supply chain is a challenge because it is everybody’s problem, but it’s also nobody’s problem.”

Another unspoken reality, according to multiple experts, is that some megaconstellation launch plans simply won’t come to fruition, at least not as originally envisioned. Space-watchers expect to see an increase in vertical integration, in which larger companies fold parts of their supply chain into themselves. But they also anticipate industry consolidation, along with some companies dropping out of the market as they find themselves unable to achieve their objectives on their own.

“Ten, 12 years ago, when the applications were submitted with the FCC for constellations of low Earth orbit satellites, no one expected all of them to move forward, and some of them just decided not to move forward with their plans,” said Doug Stroup, president of the Satellite Industry Association. “I suspect that we’ll see some of the same thing happening with respect to the recent round of applications that have been filed.”
This article first appeared in the October 2026 issue of SpaceNews Magazine.
EDITOR’S NOTE: An earlier version of this story misspelled Steve Jordan Tomaszewski. It has been updated.

articles.title: Announcing the finalists for the 2026 SpaceNews Icon Awards
articles.author: SpaceNews Editor

paras.en: The SpaceNews Icon Awards celebrate the year’s most iconic achievements in shaping the future of the space industry. Today, we’re proud to announce the shortlist for 2026 — a selection of individuals, organizations, and missions that exemplify excellence in innovation, exploration and sustainability.

This year’s honorees represent a range of accomplishments — from returning astronauts to the vicinity of the moon and expanding the capacity to run AI on orbit to accelerating the realization of on-orbit servicing and advancing scale through partnerships and acquisitions. These finalists reflect the creativity and ambition propelling today’s growth.

Winners will be announced at the 2026 SpaceNews Icon Awards on Dec. 1 in Washington D.C., where we’ll celebrate their contributions and share the stories behind their successes. In addition to recognizing this year’s winners, Space Force Gen. Michael Guetlein, direct reporting program manager for Golden Dome for America, will join us for a keynote address.
Tickets are available now – register by Oct. 31 to take advantage of our early bird rate.
Honoring individuals whose leadership and vision have left a lasting impact on the space industry, shaping exploration, national security and commercial growth for generations.

Mark Dankberg. A satellite communications pioneer who co-founded Viasat and spent decades advancing high-capacity satellite broadband, helping reshape how satellite technology connects consumers, governments and businesses.

Jean-Yves Le Gall. One of Europe’s most influential space leaders, with decades of leadership at CNES and Arianespace that helped strengthen Europe’s launch capabilities, international partnerships and position in the global space economy.

Chris Scolese. Capped a career spanning NASA and national security space after nearly seven years as director of the National Reconnaissance Office, where he oversaw a transformation of the agency’s architecture and growing integration of commercial capabilities. Scolese previously served as NASA’s chief engineer and director of Goddard Space Flight Center.

Karen St. Germain. Helped shape NASA’s Earth science enterprise through senior leadership roles overseeing missions, research and the use of satellite observations to better understand Earth’s climate and environment.

Coyote Smith. A longtime military space leader and educator whose career has helped shape thinking about spacepower, national security space strategy and the development of the next generation of space professionals.
Recognizing partnerships that bring together organizations and nations to advance space exploration, science and commerce.

Clay Mowry. Now chief executive of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA), he has worked across industry, government and professional organizations to build connections within an increasingly international and multidisciplinary space community.

Loft Orbital–Marlan Space. U.S.-French and Emirati capabilities joined in a major international space initiative, including plans for the 50-satellite Altair-Next Gen constellation combining Earth observation, onboard computing and artificial intelligence.

K2 Space–SES. Paired K2 Space’s high-power satellite platforms with SES’s software-defined payloads for meoSphere, a next-generation MEO network beginning with 28 spacecraft and designed to serve commercial and defense customers.

Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Brought together NASA, ESA, JAXA, France’s CNES, Germany’s Max Planck Institute for Astronomy and institutions across the scientific community to develop a next-generation observatory for studying dark energy, exoplanets and the evolution of the universe. Roman launched Aug. 30, beginning a new chapter in international space science.

SMILE. The Solar wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer brought ESA and the Chinese Academy of Sciences together for the first mission jointly designed, implemented, launched and operated by Europe and China. The spacecraft launched May 19 to study the interaction between the solar wind and Earth’s magnetosphere.
Recognizing new or rapidly growing companies driving innovation and opening new markets in the space economy.

Benoît Deper / Aerospacelab. Built Aerospacelab into a rapidly expanding European satellite manufacturer and operator, pursuing vertically integrated spacecraft production and constellation development from Europe and the United States.

Lux Aeterna. Emerged from stealth with plans to develop reusable satellites capable of returning payloads to Earth, raising $10 million in 2026 as it works toward its first reentry demonstration mission.

Katalyst Space Technologies. Pushed commercial satellite servicing into new territory with LINK, a rapidly developed robotic spacecraft sent to attempt the rescue of NASA’s Swift observatory, while expanding into GEO servicing, deorbiting and other robotic space operations.
Skyroot Aerospace. Advanced India’s growing private launch sector with Vikram-1, India’s first privately developed orbital-class launch vehicle.
Recognizing technologies that push the boundaries of engineering and create new capabilities for space operations.

Cailabs. Advanced laser communications from individual optical ground stations toward shared infrastructure, launching an optical-ground-station-as-a-service model with plans for an international network of roughly 15 stations.

D-Orbit. Continued expanding the capabilities of its ION orbital transfer vehicle beyond satellite deployment into hosted payloads, orbital transportation, cloud computing and other in-space logistics services.

Xona Space Systems. Advanced a commercial alternative to traditional GPS with Pulsar, a low Earth orbit positioning, navigation and timing architecture designed to provide more precise, resilient navigation services from a new generation of satellites.
Recognizing individuals whose leadership and innovation have set new benchmarks for excellence and inspired progress across the space community.

Steve Altemus, Intuitive Machines. Continued expanding Intuitive Machines from lunar transportation into a broader space infrastructure company, including the $800 million acquisition of Lanteris Space Systems and investments in communications, navigation and data services.

Ian Cinnamon, Apex. Helped establish a new model for satellite manufacturing at Apex, emphasizing standardized spacecraft platforms, faster production and an approach designed to bring mass-production economics to the satellite industry.

Rafal Modrzewski, Iceye. Led Iceye’s continued expansion of the world’s largest commercial synthetic aperture radar satellite fleet, combining commercial services with increasingly important sovereign intelligence capabilities for governments around the world.

Shey Sabripour, CesiumAstro. Built CesiumAstro around advanced active phased-array communications technology, helping move high-throughput, software-defined connectivity from a promising technology toward operational space systems.
Recognizing transactions and investments that reshape markets, create new competitors or alter the trajectory of the space industry.

AE Industrial Partners–Rocketdyne. AE Industrial agreed to acquire a controlling interest in L3Harris’ Space Propulsion and Power Systems business, reviving the Rocketdyne name for a company whose propulsion heritage stretches back more than six decades.

EQT–Exolaunch. EQT agreed to acquire Exolaunch, giving the previously self-funded German launch integration and deployment company its first outside investment and resources to expand internationally and develop new services.

Intuitive Machines–Lanteris Space Systems. Intuitive Machines completed its $800 million acquisition of the former Maxar Space Systems, adding decades of satellite manufacturing experience as it seeks to become a vertically integrated space prime.

Katalyst Space Technologies–NASA. NASA turned to Katalyst for an unusually rapid commercial servicing mission designed to rendezvous with and raise the orbit of the agency’s Swift observatory, testing a new model for acquiring time-sensitive in-space services.
SpaceX IPO. SpaceX’s long-awaited public offering brought one of the world’s most valuable private companies to public markets in a landmark transaction for the commercial space sector.
Recognizing advances that harness artificial intelligence and high-performance computing to transform spacecraft, space data and operations.
Aethero. Launched its Phobos spacecraft with an NVIDIA-powered edge-computing module, demonstrating a platform designed for continuous onboard processing and compute-as-a-service applications.

Alex Greenberg, Loft Orbital. Helped drive Loft Orbital’s push to bring artificial intelligence and high-performance computing directly into orbit, enabling satellites to process increasingly large volumes of data before sending actionable information to the ground.
Starcloud. Advanced the emerging concept of space-based data centers by developing high-performance orbital computing infrastructure intended to run increasingly demanding AI workloads in space.
Recognizing companies and missions that have advanced commercial space capabilities and contributed to the growth of the space economy.

Iceye. Expanded its synthetic aperture radar network while deploying a new generation of spacecraft capable of imagery down to 16-centimeter resolution and supporting both commercial and sovereign missions worldwide.

Impulse Space and Starfish Space. Demonstrated autonomous rendezvous and proximity operations using Impulse Space’s Mira spacecraft and Starfish Space technology, advancing commercial capabilities needed for future satellite servicing and other in-space operations.

SEOPS and Exolaunch. Expanded launch integration and rideshare services at a time of growing demand for alternatives in the commercial launch market, helping satellite operators secure access to orbit across a broader range of launch vehicles.
Recognizing leadership in using space technology to protect Earth and advancing more sustainable operations in space.

Hydrosat. Expanded the use of thermal infrared satellite data for water, agriculture and climate applications while unveiling Osiris, a next-generation constellation designed to combine 25-meter thermal imagery with broad-area coverage and daily revisit.

Space Data Association. Continued bringing satellite operators together to share operational data and promote collision avoidance, responsible operations and sustainable use of increasingly congested orbital environments.

Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Began issuing real-time scientific alerts in February, creating a system expected to eventually generate millions of alerts each night about changing objects and events ranging from asteroids to supernovae.
Celebrating breakthroughs in exploration, science and public-sector space missions.

Artemis 2 Team. Returned astronauts to the vicinity of the moon for the first time in more than half a century, carrying NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen on a nearly 10-day flight around the moon aboard Orion. The April mission brought together NASA, international partners and a vast industrial team supporting Orion, the Space Launch System and ground systems.

Copernicus Sentinel-1D Team. Brought Sentinel-1D into full operations in May, restoring and strengthening Europe’s flagship radar Earth observation capability and continuing more than a decade of global environmental monitoring through Copernicus.

Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Team. Successfully launched NASA’s next flagship astrophysics observatory Aug. 30, beginning a mission designed to survey the universe far faster than Hubble while investigating dark energy, exoplanets and some of astronomy’s biggest unanswered questions.
Recognizing individuals, organizations and missions making significant contributions to national security space capabilities.

Gurpartap “GP” Sandhoo. Took leadership of the Space Development Agency while also becoming the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for missile warning and tracking, overseeing deployment of the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture and its growing constellation of military satellites.

Impulse Space. Expanded its national security role with a $28 million Space Force contract for a future space domain awareness mission using its highly maneuverable Mira spacecraft in low Earth orbit.

SpaceWERX. Continued using the Space Force’s small-business innovation programs to move emerging commercial technologies toward military applications and broaden the pool of companies contributing to national security space.

VICTUS HAZE Team. Demonstrated the Space Force’s most advanced tactically responsive space mission to date, with Rocket Lab and True Anomaly spacecraft supporting realistic rendezvous and proximity operations and space domain awareness scenarios after a rapid-response launch campaign.
Join us for the 2026 SpaceNews Icon Awards in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 1.

articles.title: Oct. 29: Applying AI to the GEOINT Mission
articles.author: SpaceNews Editor

paras.en: Artificial intelligence is changing how intelligence organizations collect, process and exploit satellite imagery. As the volume of Earth observation data grows, AI is becoming essential for identifying patterns, detecting anomalies and delivering intelligence at operational speed.
Join SpaceNews and Vantor on Oct. 29 for a virtual event that will explore how machine learning is transforming the GEOINT mission across defense, intelligence and commercial markets.

Speakers will discuss advances in automated target recognition, change detection, multimodal data fusion and large language models, as well as the challenges of validating AI outputs and maintaining analyst trust. The conversation will consider where AI delivers its greatest operational value, where humans remain indispensable and how intelligence organizations can adapt to persistent, data-driven surveillance.
- Peter Wilczynski, chief product officer, Vantor
- Joe O’Callaghan, director, Super Intelligence (SI) Mission, National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency
- Matt Maroofi, senior director of product, Shield AI
This virtual event will take place via Zoom. You will receive a unique link to join with your registration confirmation. A recording will be posted here shortly after the event concludes.

Vantor is forging the new frontier of spatial intelligence to unlock a more autonomous, interoperable world. We give decision makers and operators the power to build a unified intelligence picture, delivering the clarity they need to navigate what’s happening now and shape what’s coming next. We fuse data from our constellation, which includes the most capable imaging satellites on orbit, with real-time sensor feeds from space, air, and ground to create an AI-ready digital twin of Earth. Our spatial intelligence platform automates every part of the cycle—from tasking to collection to production—to update and analyze this foundation at the pace of change. Our products drive deeper mission-critical insights and connect the next generation of autonomous systems across the defense, intelligence, and commercial landscape. To learn more, visit www.vantor.com

articles.title: NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño

paras.en: A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific.

As of October, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has said that there's an 83% chance that the strongest El Niño since 1950 is currently unfolding. People around the world, including farmers, firefighters, and coastal communities, are already experiencing the effects in different ways.
Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Niño from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

One of the first clues appeared in satellite imagery in January 2026, when a swell of warm water called a Kelvin wave was spotted near Micronesia in the western Pacific. Kelvin waves are slow-moving pulses of water thousands of miles long. Like underwater freeways, they transfer heat from west to east across the Pacific. The warm water heats the air directly above it, making it rise. The change in air pressures weakens or even reverses the trade winds that typically blow in the opposing direction, from the Americas toward Asia, causing sea levels in the eastern Pacific to rise further, and waters to warm even more. This chain reaction signifies the start of an El Niño.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The map above shows that by early April, those Kelvin waves had reached the eastern Pacific, and sea surface temperatures had begun to warm. Warm water expands in volume, elevating local sea levels in some areas by as much as 1 to 1.3 feet (30 to 40 centimeters). The higher-than-normal water can be seen sloshing toward South America then moving up the coast to California. Sea levels that are six to eight inches (15 to 20 centimeters) lower than normal are visible around Indonesia and northern Australia.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Kelvin waves are like the heartbeat of El Niño,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “And our sea level satellites let us peer into the ocean and watch every beat.”

Scientists have used satellite altimetry to track the height of the ocean with ultraprecision since 1993. That unbroken data record continues today with the Sentinel-6 satellites. State-of-the-art radar altimeters aboard these satellites survey millions of square miles of ocean in a single day, complementing NOAA’s fleet of ocean sensors and buoys drifting and diving through the water below.

Warmer-than-normal seawater is one of the best-known indicators of El Niño. Already, sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific are about 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.7 degrees Celsius) warmer than the long-term average and could jump another fraction of a degree in the coming months, Willis said.

Satellites carrying microwave and infrared radiometers can see through and around clouds to measure heat energy at the sea surface. Satellites in 2026 mapped the band of warmer-than-normal water as it expanded throughout the spring. The band, seen in dark red, stretches for millions of square miles from the heart of the Pacific to the coast of South America. Ocean temperatures can influence weather patterns around the world. Air above the water’s surface carries heat and moisture into the atmosphere, seeding rainstorms and rearranging weather patterns across the globe.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: El Niño’s warm waters also change the color of the ocean. A NASA satellite is tracking these subtle shifts in hues, as equatorial Pacific waters have become measurably more blue over the last several months.

“Some people think of water as being just blue, but it's amazing the multitude of colors the ocean can be,” said Matthew Kehrli, a lead research scientist for the PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite team at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

This spectrum is in part thanks to microscopic plants called phytoplankton, which form the basis of the marine food web. There are thousands of different species of phytoplankton, which come in shades like teal, brown, or green. This year, in areas of the Pacific Ocean along the equator that are typically lush with phytoplankton and greener as a result, these hues are waning.

This is an expected effect of El Niño. Phytoplankton thrive in cool, nutrient-rich waters, but during an El Niño, the weakening trade winds reduce the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface. With limited food supply, phytoplankton abundance drops. This decline can trigger cascading effects across the marine food web, forcing other marine life to relocate to new feeding grounds.

This year’s El Niño is the first since PACE launched in 2024, providing new views of the phenomenon. The Ocean Color Instrument aboard PACE observes the ocean in hyperspectral color — across several hundred different wavelengths of visible, near-infrared, and ultraviolet light — monitoring phytoplankton and other ocean-color changes in near-real time. With PACE data, researchers calculate the average color of the ocean, simplifying spectra of light into a single number, known as apparent visible wavelength.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The 2026 map above shows the green area along the equator in the western Pacific Ocean shrink as a bluer shade fills in, indicating fewer phytoplankton. In contrast, the map from 2025 shows how the green-hued section stays steady over time.
“You have expectations of what you would think would happen,” Kehrli said. “But to visually see the results with the data products that you’re working with in real time is gratifying.”
NASA scientists will continue to monitor the signs and impacts of this El Niño with its fleet of Earth-observing satellites.
“El Niño touches almost all of us in some way every time it occurs,” Willis said. “While many have seen what it can do, we look to the ocean to understand why.”
View and download these data visualizations here.

articles.title: NASA to Help Unlock Mysteries of Mars’ Moons in Upcoming Mission

paras.en: NASA is playing an important role in JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of Mars’ moons and build on the agency’s long history of exploring the Red Planet.

The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of Mars’ moons Phobos and Deimos and deliver a sample of Phobos to Earth. The MMX spacecraft is targeting launch from JAXA’s Tanegashima Space Center in Japan at 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. JST on Tuesday, Oct. 20).

“The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “The NASA-JAXA sample curation partnership is extremely valuable, and I am proud that NASA Science is supporting MMX sample curation and will be sharing portions of these samples for study as we continue to expand humanity’s understanding of the universe for the benefit of all.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: NASA’s contributions to the mission include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE) spectrograph instrument, the Pneumatic Sampler (P-Sampler) technology demonstration, and communications and navigation support from the agency’s Deep Space Network, as well as funding United States scientists participating on the MMX science team.

Scientists have long debated the origin of Mars’ two moons. The data and samples collected by the MMX mission will help answer essential questions about the origins of these moons and the history of the solar system.

“Phobos and Deimos may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars’ gravity billions of years ago,” said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters. “Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds.”

The MEGANE (pronounced meh-GAH-nay, the Japanese word for eyeglasses) spectrograph will help scientists “see” what Phobos is made of by measuring neutrons and gamma rays emitted from the moon’s surface and determining its chemical elemental composition, which will provide important clues about its origin.

Mounted on one of the spacecraft’s landing legs, the P-Sampler is designed to collect a ground sample from Phobos. The system gathers surface material using bursts of high-pressure nitrogen gas, complementing JAXA’s C-Sampler, which will extract cores from a few inches deeper. NASA will obtain and curate about 15% of the total returned sample at the agency’s Johnson Space Center Astromaterials Lab in Houston, making it available for research for decades.

Another key part of NASA’s contribution to MMX is its scientific partnership with JAXA. NASA-supported researchers are working alongside international colleagues to help reveal the story of Phobos and will use mission data and returned samples to uncover new clues about the moon’s origin and the evolution of the Mars system.

The MMX spacecraft will arrive at Mars in August 2027 to begin its survey of the Red Planet’s two moons. After surveying Phobos in detail, the spacecraft will collect a sample of the moon’s surface no earlier than December 2028 and deliver it to Earth in 2031.

The MEGANE instrument was developed by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory. Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, developed the spacecraft’s pneumatic sampler mechanism. NASA’s contributions to the MMX mission were developed under the agency’s Discovery Program. The Discovery Program is managed by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, for the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington.
For more information about the MMX mission, visit:
karen.c.fox@nasa.gov / alana.r.johnson@nasa.gov

articles.title: Isaias Dims the Gulf Coast

paras.en: After a quiet start to the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, Isaias became the season’s first hurricane on October 8 as it tracked toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. The storm brought heavy rain and flash flooding to parts of the Southeast, including Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, and winds that toppled trees and downed power lines, leaving many people in the dark.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the evening of October 9 as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles (170 kilometers) per hour. Gusts topped 100 miles per hour along a corridor west of the storm’s center, according to the National Weather Service, with preliminary reports showing a 117-mile-per-hour gust in Oriole Beach and a 102-mile-per-hour gust at Pensacola City Hall.

These areas of high winds overlapped a broader area west of the storm’s eye where satellite images showed substantial decreases in nighttime lights. The image pair above shows nighttime lights before and after the storm. The left image is a composite of August 2026 data representing typical conditions, and the right image shows lights on October 11, after most of the storm’s clouds had cleared.

The data depicted in the images, provided by Ranjay Shrestha of NASA's Black Marble science team, come from the Black Marble HD product. The product uses data from the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite, which has a day-night band that detects light emitted and reflected at night. The team processed the data to account for changes in the landscape, the atmosphere, and phase of the Moon, and to filter out stray light that does not come from electric lights. Dark gray, hash-marked areas show where clouds prevented VIIRS from collecting data. The nighttime lights are shown over a base map from the Landsat 9 satellite.

paras.en: “Standard Black Marble nighttime lights imagery, available through NASA Worldview, provides a broad picture of the storm's immediate impacts,” Shrestha said. “Black Marble HD takes this a step further by allowing us to visualize these changes at a much finer spatial scale.”

At these finer scales, the images reveal lights decreasing sharply around parts of Pensacola, Florida, and along the U.S. Route 98 corridor toward Destin, suggesting widespread power disruptions. Shrestha also pointed out pockets where lights persisted, including Pensacola International Airport, Pensacola Christian College, and parts of downtown Pensacola. “These patterns could reflect backup power systems, differences in electrical infrastructure, or areas that maintained electricity during the storm, although the imagery alone cannot confirm the underlying reasons,” he said.

paras.en: Black Marble HD images also reveal the pace and spatial patterns of recovery. The image pair above compares the same October 11 view (left) with one from October 12 (right), when lights had begun to return to some affected areas. By October 14, lighting patterns looked similar to pre-storm conditions.

“Understanding where recovery is progressing and where disruptions persist can help emergency responders and decision makers identify areas that may require additional attention, prioritize resources, and assess the effectiveness of restoration efforts,” Shrestha said.

Black Marble data complement ground-based outage reports rather than replace them, offering a more comprehensive view of disasters' impacts and recovery. “Ultimately, this is where the value of Black Marble lies: turning nighttime Earth observations into actionable insights that support informed decisions and help bridge the gap between Earth science and action,” Shrestha said.

The NASA Disasters Program, in coordination with FEMA and the USGS Coastal Storms Team, is supporting the Alabama Red Cross and the Alabama Emergency Management Agency’s response to Hurricane Isaias. The team will be posting maps and data products on its open-access mapping portal as new information becomes available.

articles.title: AI, green energy and economic transitions risk leaving vulnerable communities behind, UN warns

paras.en: AI, green energy and economic transitions risk leaving vulnerable communities behind, UN warns

Rapid transformations – from artificial intelligence and digital technologies to renewable energy and demographic shifts – are reshaping economies worldwide, creating new opportunities but also threatening to deepen socio-economic inequalities, a new UN report warned on Thursday.
Benefiting from these changes often requires specialised skills and access to the latest technologies, putting disadvantaged groups at risk of being left behind.

Women, young people, older persons, persons with disabilities, migrants, Indigenous Peoples and low-income communities are particularly vulnerable, the report stresses, outlining recommendations for governments to ensure these transformations benefit everyone.
Social inclusion is a moral imperative, but it is also an economic necessity, the report from the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) underlined.

It found that expanding opportunities to marginalised groups enlarges the productive workforce, strengthens human capital, increases innovation and entrepreneurship, improves labour allocation and spreads productivity gains more widely.
“Inclusive societies are more productive, resilient, and prosperous,” Secretary-General António Guterres summarised in a video message for the launch of the report.
Measures towards social inclusion should also be taken urgently, as those left outside key systems face steeper barriers to catching up later, the report emphasised.

As artificial intelligence transforms labour markets, the report urges governments to invest in continuous training and reskilling for workers whose jobs may be replaced or transformed, rather than focusing solely on creating new jobs.
Similarly, the shift to renewable energy must include support for workers and communities reliant on fossil fuels, through retraining, alternative employment opportunities and social assistance.
To bridge the digital divide, governments should also expand affordable access to the internet, digital infrastructure and technology training – particularly in disadvantaged communities.

One last major recommendation is to stop relying mainly on GDP to evaluate growth, and to also assess progress through poverty reduction, access to education and healthcare, employment security, inequality and environmental protection.
Economic growth that benefits only a small share of the population, it argues, cannot be considered genuinely inclusive.
Importantly, these investments require resources and many developing countries are facing financial constraints that could hamper the transition.

Nearly half of the world’s poorest countries are either in or at high risk of debt distress, with interest payments relative to revenue at their highest levels in a generation, the UN Secretary-General warned.
He called on leaders to live up to the commitments made through last year’s Doha Political Declaration on Social Development and the Sevilla Commitment on financing for development.
He also pushed for reform of international financial institutions to better represent and serve developing countries.
“Transformations are inevitable. Inequality and exclusion are not,” the UN Secretary-General said.
“Let’s work together to ensure that the profound transformations reshaping our world help build societies rooted in justice, dignity and opportunity for all.”

articles.title: The world is waging a ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags

paras.en: The world is waging a ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags

Fewer than half of the national targets set to protect the world’s plants, animals and ecosystems are on track, the UN warns in a new report, days before countries gather in Yerevan, Armenia, for the COP17 biodiversity conference.
The landmark deal struck in Montreal in 2022 – the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework – set out a vision of “living in harmony with nature” by 2050, with urgent action needed by 2030.
The new report suggests the world is falling behind.

“Biodiversity underpins life on Earth,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in the report. “Safeguarding biological diversity is essential to the health of our planet, the resilience of our economies and the wellbeing of all people.”
One of the deal’s flagship goals was to protect at least 30 per cent of the world’s land, inland waters, coasts and oceans by 2030.
Yet even if current commitments are met, only 26 per cent of land and 12 per cent of the ocean would be protected by that deadline, the report finds.
Progress is also lagging on money, skills, cooperation and data, as well as on economic incentives that reward protecting nature rather than destroying it.
“This bad news means that the war on nature has not yet ended,” Mr. Guterres said at the report’s launch in Yerevan.
He warned that the world is still caught in three interlinked crises: climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
There has been some progress since 2022, however.
Nearly 90 per cent of countries that are parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have set national targets, and more than half have drawn up their own plans to deliver them.
More than 70 per cent have measured and reported on their results.

Indigenous Peoples, local communities, regional and city authorities, charities and businesses have also made some 5,000 commitments – though the report warns of a serious gap between ambition and action.
Closing that gap will require money and expertise for developing countries on a far bigger scale, the report says.
Governments need to scrap subsidies that harm nature, strengthen social protection, redirect spending towards protecting nature and work with businesses on strong disclosure rules.
Better coordination is also needed between governments, business, civil society, young people, women and Indigenous Peoples to strengthen accountability, enforcement and cooperation.
“Biodiversity must be part of every decision being made – across policies, regulations and budgets,” Mr. Guterres said.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions.”

articles.title: Could your brain data be used against you? UN calls for limits on neurotechnology

paras.en: Could your brain data be used against you? UN calls for limits on neurotechnology

Brain signals recorded by a gaming headset or a wellness gadget could one day be used as evidence against you in court, according to a new UN report which warns that neurotechnology is outpacing the laws meant to protect human rights.

Presenting the Secretary-General’s report to the General Assembly on Thursday, senior human rights official Claudia Fuentes Julio said the technology could threaten privacy, freedom of thought and the right to a fair trial, particularly for marginalised people.
- The new report examines the growing use of neurotechnology in justice systems and the risks arising from its convergence with artificial intelligence (AI)
- Data collected through gaming or wellness devices, for instance, could be used in a court of law, impacting fundamental human rights, including the right to a fair trial
- The report calls for prohibiting coercive and abusive applications of neurotechnology and establishing stronger legal and ethical safeguards
Neurotechnology was once exclusively used for medical diagnoses or treatment, measuring, monitoring, analysing, predicting or modulating the nervous system.
The new tech gathers neural data – defined as qualitative and quantitative data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system.

“Neurotechnology accesses, measures and analyses brain signals,” the UN chief wrote in his report. “If these signals are treated as direct indicators of thoughts, intentions or truthfulness, the use of neural data points could undermine how we understand and value each of us as human beings.”

Once confined to clinical or research environments, these devices are now entering, or may enter, consumer markets, workplaces, schools, public services, law enforcement and justice systems, the report found.

UN Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights Claudia Fuentes Julio highlighted a range of risks when introducing the report to Third Committee members, including the growing commercialisation of neurotechnology and the collection of large volumes of neural data by technology companies.
Marketed for wellness, gaming and productivity, wearable, so-called electroencephalography devices are now increasingly available.

As such, neural data collected through these devices could be accessed by governments or introduced as evidence in legal proceedings without adequate recognition of its highly sensitive nature, the report warned.

While these new technologies hold significant promise, particularly for medical and assistive applications, Ms. Fuentes Julio said the report “warns of risks to dignity, privacy, freedom of thought, fair trial rights, liberty and protection from ill-treatment, especially for marginalised groups”.

Indeed, when applied in the courtroom these technologies serve different purposes and pose distinct legal and human rights risks, especially as tools and data developed for medical use are repurposed without appropriate safeguards, the report argues.

Ms. Fuentes Julio said the report calls for “prohibitions on coercive and abusive uses, and stronger safeguards, informed consent, scientific validation, oversight, accountability and protection of neural data.”
The report emphasises that neural data, as “uniquely sensitive personal data,” demands heightened protection.

articles.title: Rutter scores twice as Brighton win big and go top in Conference League

paras.en: Brighton and Hove Albion vs Kauno Zalgiris; UEFA Conference League
Brighton and Hove Albion vs Kauno Zalgiris. UEFA Conference League.
Brighton 4-0 Kauno Zalgiris: Georginio Rutter scores twice as Seagulls thrash Lithuanian side in Conference League

Match report as Brighton thrash Kauno Zalgris to get off to flying start in Conference League; Georginio Rutter scores two and gets an assist, with Jack Hinshelwood and Matt O’Riley also on target for Fabian Hurzeler’s side who go top of the standings
Georginio Rutter scored twice and set up one as Brighton thrashed Kauno Zalgris 4-0 to get their Conference League campaign off to a winning start.

Brighton were dominant from the first whistle to the last against the Lithuanian Cup winners and took the lead through Rutter, but only after a VAR check. The ball had initially been deemed to have gone out of play before Ibrahim Osman's cut-back to the Frenchman, but the goal was awarded after review.

Rutter then turned provider as Brighton doubled their lead on the stroke of half-time when Hinshelwood - returning to the side for the first time since the Premier League opening weekend - slotted into the corner.
The third came after a lung-bursting run from Malick Yalcouye, who played Osman through to cross for Rutter to turn into the net with ease.

articles.title: Bournemouth beat Sturm Graz in first ever home European game

paras.en: Bournemouth vs Sturm Graz; UEFA Europa League
Bournemouth vs Sturm Graz. UEFA Europa League.
Bournemouth 3-0 Sturm Graz: Cherries win first ever home European game as they make it two from two in Europa League

Match report as Bournemouth win their first-ever home European game, beating Sturm Graz; Evanilson scored at the end of the first half to hand the Cherries the lead; Rayan and an Alvaro Rodriguez penalty added after the break; Bournemouth face AC Milain in the Europa League next Thursday
Bournemouth's history-making season continued on Thursday as they played - and won - their first-ever home European match, beating Sturm Graz 3-0 in the Europa League.

It makes it two wins from two for the competition debutants and perhaps more importantly, they held on to a lead they took towards the end of the first half - something they have been unable to do in a poor start to the Premier League.

Evanilson will go down as the man who scored the first European goal at the Vitality Stadium and it was a thing of beauty. Adam Smith - captaining a team he joined in England's third tier 16 years ago - found him with a cross, with the Brazilian curling a powerful header past the goalkeeper from 15 yards out.
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream Premier League games with no contract📺

Sturm Graz came out with intent at the start of the second half and could have equalised just after the hour. Jurgen Heil smashed the woodwork before Djorde Petrovic was needed to keep out Jacob Hodl's follow-up.

But the Cherries rode the wave and doubled their lead through another Brazilian, Rayan. It was a howler from Daniil Khudyakov, whose spilled save from a corner landed to the Bournemouth forward. His low, fizzing shot then sped through the goalkeeper's outstretched hands.

And in second-half added time, Bournemouth were awarded a penalty. Former Huddersfield man Jon Gorenc Stankovic was penalised for a foul on James Hill - also coming in the aftermath of a Bournemouth corner.

Summer signing Alvaro Rodriguez stepped up to chip the spot kick in for his first Bournemouth goal, sealing another three points. It puts the Cherries fifth in the Europa League league phase table ahead of welcoming Ruben Amorim's AC Milan to the Vitality next Thursday.
Key moments from the Vitality Stadium...

43: GOAL! Evanilson gives Bournemouth the lead with an incredible curling header from some distance.
63: OFF THE POST! SAVE! Heil hits the post with a thunderous effort from the right, before Hodl's follow-up is stopped by Djorde Petrovic's legs.
76: GOAL! Rayan's low, hard shot beats Khudyakov after some poor goalkeeping.
90+2: PENALTY SCORED! Stankovic fouls Hill as he strikes inside the box and Bournemouth are awarded a penalty. Rodriguez scores from the spot.
Bournemouth captain Adam Smith to TNT Sports: "It's been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we're very happy with the performance.

"It wasn't my best cross [for Evanilson's goal], but I put it into the area and what a finish from him. It's a great header. He's deserved it because he's worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.
"We deserved that bit of luck and from there, we went on to win the game. In the second half, we got a bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great. We look forward to Sunday now."

On if this can be a springboard for Bournemouth: "It was very disappointing at the weekend [against Chelsea]. We let ourselves down as players, we know that. We had a chat with each other and got a reaction today.
"That's a Bournemouth performance right there, but the week is not done. We have a massive game against Sunderland and we need to get three points."
Rose: A deserved win - now we have to be consistent

Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose to TNT Sports when asked if he saw what he wanted from his team: "Yes. Performance wise, clean sheet, attitude, effort. A deserved win and now we have to continue and get consistent in this kind of thing. Sunderland is the next challenge.
"I believe in this team and I know we are always confident, despite being in a difficult situation [in the Premier League]. Even today, we changed some players.
"We could see that the squad is working, that everyone is keen to play, that everyone deserves to play and it's good for us for the next few weeks to have a competitive squad.
"Today, we won 3-0 and it's a really good result after a good performance, but we have to prove it [consistency].
"Alvaro Rodriguez did some steps the last three weeks which began with the national break. He worked really hard individually and you could see every step and I'm quite happy that he scored.

"If we stick together like this, if we have our fans then we are hard to play [against] and then it's hard to beat us. That's what we should take into the next game. It's getting tough one but it helps this kind of game, this result."
'This needs to be a springboard for Bournemouth's season'
Analysis from Sky Sports News' Mark McAdam at the Vitality: "Back-to-back wins in the Europa League!

"Not a classic by any stretch but one that will live long in the memories for Bournemouth fans; their first ever taste of European football at the Vitality - a real moment in history. A game they dominated across the pitch from start to finish.
"This needs to be the springboard for their season and their next match against Sunderland in the Premier League on Sunday. Win that and suddenly their season is off and running..."

articles.title: Britain faces ‘new era’ of security threats from Iran and Russia, MI5 says
articles.author: Alexander Smith

paras.en: LONDON — Iran is escalating its campaign of threats on British soil, expanding attacks beyond dissidents abroad and Jewish sites to now focusing on harder military targets, the country’s domestic intelligence chief said Tuesday.

MI5 Director General Ken McCallum was speaking less than two weeks after the United States rushed to withdraw its bombers from a key air base in England, with American officials saying there had been reports of a possible Iranian drone attack.

Giving a wide-ranging “annual threat update” at MI5’s Thames House headquarters in London, McCallum warned that Britain and Europe had “entered a new era of national security,” which he likened to the shift that came after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

His speech comes at a moment of tumult not just for the Middle East and Ukraine, which continue to be ravaged by war, but also the rest of Europe, which has suffered so-called hybrid aggression from Moscow and Tehran including sabotage, arson and cyberattacks. European governments are now openly telling people to stockpile food and prepare for more of their taxes to be spent on defense, warning that Russia may launch a direct attack on their soil.
MI5 is now devoting more resources than it had during the Cold War to countering threats from countries such as Russia, Iran, China and others, McCallum said.
“Russia remains aggressor No. 1, as Putin’s Kremlin continues to lash out at the U.K. and its allies,” he added.

But another arch belligerent is Iran, whose leaders have been “attempting to expand their hybrid campaign” of “using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations and Israeli sites,” the spy chief said.

“Much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities, with whom I want to express solidarity,” he said. But this year has seen a shift of “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.”
Over the past year, intelligence operations have led to more than 50 Iran-linked arrests in Britain, he said.

McCallum made reference to the incident last month at RAF Fairford, the military base in rural England from where the U.S. had been launching bombers involved in the assault against Iran. He declined to give details, citing ongoing investigations and operations, but said the case was “not unique.”

Details are hazy, but in the early hours of Sept. 27, a member of the public called the police after spotting three vans in a country lane near the base. Seven men in their 20s, one of them a dual British-Iranian national, have been arrested and released on bail. Authorities said they found only gasoline in the vehicles.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in Parliament on Monday that the incident “is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed” by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the powerful political, military and economic group that holds huge sway in the country.
A week after the incident, Washington hastily withdrew its bombers from the base because, according to two U.S. officials, of reports of a possible drone attack against the site.

On Tuesday, McCallum downplayed fears that Iran could mount such a complex attack, saying it has so far been hiring unsophisticated criminals for operations in the United Kingdom. But he warned that could change.

On Russia, McCallum said its military and intelligence services “are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare,” being careful not to trigger NATO’s Article 5 threshold, in which other countries would be expected to defend their allies.
“We see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding,” he said. “The whole aim of hybrid tactics is to try to intimidate us.”

Within the U.K.’s “multifaceted relationship with China” — Beijing is a major trading partner to London — MI5 has been focused on efforts by the Chinese government “to conduct espionage, coercion or democratic interference.”
On Al Qaeda and the Islamic State terrorist group, or ISIS, MI5 still has to respond “to attempts to carry out mass casualty attacks,” he said.
But perhaps the gravest warning came when it came to artificial intelligence, which he said in the future could be used by terrorist groups and other actors to create new “bioweapons.”
And “beyond misuse of AI by human adversaries sit the potential risks posed by AI itself,” he said.

“Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are. Is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel. And deserves the serious attention it is getting, including in MI5.”

articles.title: Why advanced U.S. weapons aren’t stopping Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia

paras.en: Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology.

But in recent days it has appeared helpless in the face of barrages of missiles and drones fired by the Houthi rebel group from neighboring Yemen. The attacks have struck Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors and work from home.

The Iran-backed Houthis, once seen as little more than a ragtag militia, have grown into a formidable fighting force. They have inflicted damage on the region’s top oil producer, threatened critical supply routes in the Red Sea and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands.

The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defenses failed to stop the Houthis’ attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict:

Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12% of all U.S. arms exports from 2021 to 2025.

Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defense systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers.
Saudi Arabia’s annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles.
The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia’s large size.

Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country’s sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles through rugged desert areas.

“Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday.
At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help.
Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support.
President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision.

Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn’t require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting.
The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defenses.

The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023. While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year.

Andreas Krieg, a professor at King’s College London, said this experience in challenging Israel’s cutting-edge air defenses has given the Houthis confidence and expertise as they now strike Saudi Arabia.
“They’ve learned how to oversaturate the radars,” he said.

The Houthis, working with allied militias in Iraq, have also targeted Saudi oil installations, including a vital pipeline used to export oil through the Red Sea while movement through the Strait of Hormuz is limited. The Houthis have also seized territory in Yemen near the Bab el-Mandeb, a key Red Sea waterway, putting additional pressure on Saudi oil exports.
Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, says the kingdom assumed the Houthis wouldn’t strike civilian targets like airports. Doing so marked “a paradigm shift,” he said.

Ratney, now an adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Saudis now find themselves in a position where they have to respond while also trying to prevent the fighting from spinning out of control.
“They can’t not strike back — they were attacked in a very brutal way by their archenemies,” he said. “They need to exert military pressure on the Houthis and then find a way to kind of de-escalate.”
Rather than sending troops into Yemen, the Saudis will likely launch airstrikes against the Houthis and ramp up support of nationalist forces, several analysts said.
“It will be surrogate warfare,” Krieg said.
While the Houthis don’t have the firepower of Saudi Arabia, they have grown into a fearsome force controlling roughly one-third of Yemen thanks to help from Iran.

The United Nations estimates that the Houthis by 2024 had recruited up to 350,000 fighters. That’s up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in the internationally recognized Yemeni government’s civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade.
Ratney says the Houthis now have a “symbiotic relationship” with Iran and should not be seen as an Iranian puppet.

The strikes on Saudi airports and economic assets symbolize a sharing of lessons in asymmetric warfare between the Houthis and the Iranians: how to not just puncture expensive air defenses, but also damage vulnerable energy installations and threaten global maritime routes.

“Over the course of the past few years, the Iranians have been innovating and sharing that with the Houthis and it’s gone both ways. The Houthis have been innovating, and sharing it with the Iranians,” Ratney said. “It’s no coincidence that they’ve ended up with a similar approach.”
Their recent military successes have made the Houthis feel “untouchable,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a fellow at Chatham House focused on Yemen.

“It’s very hard to convince a man he’s going on the wrong side if he just moved forward and he has a gun in his hand,” he said. But the Houthis are now likely to suffer a brutal Saudi counterattack, he said.
